newsitem.title: UK: NatWest firmer after corporate loan plans.
newsitem.headline: NatWest firmer after corporate loan plans.

text.p: Shares in National Westminster Bank rose on Wednesday after it said that it planned to securitise about five billion dollars of its corporate loans to release capital to the banking group, analysts said.
By 0750 GMT the shares had added 5p to 666-1/2p.

Overnight news that the U.S. Federal Reserve had decided to leave interest rates unchanged also helped lift banking stocks across the board as prices rebounded from Tuesday's bout of profit-taking ahead of the rate decision.
Barclays shares rose 4-1/2p to 937p, Royal Bank of Scotland 12p to 483-1/2p and LLoyds 5p to 376-1/2p.

The initial significance of the NatWest move was small, analysts said. NatWest already has a high Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio and will raise it by about 200 million stg by freeing capital via the removal of loans from the balance sheet.
It also means that the reduction in future capital needed to support and expand the loan book will increase free cash flow by about 10 million stg a year on an ongoing basis, analysts said.

"It's a sound strategic move getting assets off the balance sheet but the capital significance initially and ongoing is reasonably small in terms of the group," said ABN AMRO Hoare Govett banking analyst Steven Thorn.

"The real interest is that it shows Natwest, after many years of lagging Barclays' strategy of very aggressively removing low margin loans from its balance sheet, are taking a very firm step in the same direction," he said.
The move signalled that NatWest management were now committed to policies focused on shareholder value and as such was very good news, added Thorn.

The transaction means NatWest will transform corporate loans into stg and dollar-denominated floating rate notes and commercial paper, issued into the Eurobond market as well as the U.S. 144A private placement market.
NatWest said the securitisation would improve its Tier 1 ratio by about 0.2 percent. The ratio stood at 7.6 in July when the bank reported its first-half results.
NatWest will start presentations to investors in London, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Bahrain, Dublin, Frankfurt and Luxembourg in early October to sell the securities.
But NatWest's move is unlikely to spark a wave of securitisation in the industry with Barclays, in particular, already having done much to remove low margin lending from its balance sheet.
The process itself is not innovative, though the size is, which, said Thorn, showed the commitment of Natwest to improving the return on the balance sheet and adding to shareholder value.
"Almost whatever they do with the money -- unless they make a very low return acquisition -- will increase shareholder value," said Thorn.
"This is just another piece in the jigsaw to suggest NatWest has turned the corner and that the large discount of the shares to the rest of the sector is unsustainable in the medium term."
